ng_guide.text: Newgrange: built about 3200 BC, with roughly 200,000 tonnes of stone and earth. That's five hundred years older than the Great Pyramid and a thousand older than Stonehenge.
The white quartz on the front was brought from Wicklow, fifty-odd miles off, and the grey stones from the Boyne. On a bright day, the whole thing glitters like a very big, very old iPhone.

lottery_winner.text: Every year around 30,000 people enter the lottery for the winter solstice. Fifty get in, two at a time. I'm the first Munster winner since 1994.
You stand in the dark, and then a thin line of gold comes down the passage. They say it's just the sun. I say it's still astonishing.

ng_farmer.text: My family's farmed beside this tomb for generations. We found stones in the field every year. Mostly we put them back. They looked cross.
There are three tombs: Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth. Knowth has more carved stones than anywhere else in Europe. I've only half the facts, but I've all the pride.

ng_archaeologist.text: Professor O'Kelly led the dig and rebuilding in the 1960s and 70s. The quartz wall's controversial, but I'm told the roof really does keep out the rain.
After five thousand years, the roof of the chamber has never once leaked. The Neolithic builders would be insulted you asked.

spiral_kid.text: There are three spirals joined at the middle, on the big stone at the door. I drew it on my hand with a pen. Mam says I'm not allowed near the stones.
I think it's a map. Or a bus route. Or the world's first doodle.

then.text: I'm going to stay a while. Go and see the North. I'll keep the kettle warm. Somewhere in Ireland I'll find a kettle.

else.text: A woman in a cardigan, anorak and walking boots stands on the grass by the great kerbstone, holding a flask and looking up at the mound as if it owed her money.
{player}! There you are. Professor Elspeth Garside, in the flesh, so to speak. I hired a car. It has a gearstick. I didn't know they still had those.
I felt it from the car park. The whole mound rang like a bell. That wasn't the Wardstone. That was her. Oh, that was her.
Seven Stones. Ten legends in the isles, and you've woken a good few. That's more than the whole of the old Society managed. They'd be furious. They'd also be jealous.
Kerrigan's on a bench by the car park with a 99. She says it's the first ice cream she's had since 2019. Be kind. She's had a long week, and so have the crows.
Now. The North. Belfast, the Causeway, the Mournes. The Iron Stone, I think, and a lot of very old basalt. And Scotland beyond. The hum there is a deep, slow one.
The North is waiting. But rest first, and visit the Dragon. And take a flask. I always say that. I'm told it's a catchphrase.
Oh, {player}, one more thing. I've been meaning to tell you for an hour. Hold on, it's easier if I ring you.
Her phone is in her hand. Yours buzzes anyway. She waves at you, three feet away, and carries on.
Your phone buzzes. Professor Garside, who is somewhere with a great deal of wind in it.
{player}! It's me. Don't panic. The signal's good for once and the crows won't stop talking.
At first light something tall and feathered went up out of the Boyne and flew north. Over the Mournes, a farmer says, with three crows for an escort and no regard for the airspace.
The Morrígan, I'd say. Or her shadow, if you've got her with you. She's a goddess of war and fate. She keeps more than one diary.

North is where the hum is going. Belfast first: there's a Keeper in the shipyard, Ruairí, with the Iron Stone. Then the Giant's Causeway, where I'm told Lord Vane himself has been seen with a clipboard.

The road leaves the Boyne Valley over the Mournes. Mind the Mourne Wall. It runs up and down every hill for twenty-two miles, and as far as I can tell it keeps the sheep out of the reservoir and the sheep amused.
Pack warm things. And take a flask. I always say that. I'm told it's a catchphrase.
The way north is open: the Mournes, and Belfast beyond.

kerrigan_after.text: It's a 99. With a flake. It's a good flake. Do you know, I've been in this job six years and I've never once eaten one outdoors.
I've handed in the lanyard. HR said it was the strangest exit interview they'd ever had. I said that was fair. I was interviewed by a crow.
I'll go home to Navan and see my mother. I'll tell her I've quit a job. She'll say 'about time', and then she'll put the kettle on.
